entities.summary:
Andrea Bianco, an accomplished Italian navigator and cartographer who died around 1500, played a pivotal role in the evolution of maritime mapping during the late Medieval and early Renaissance periods. Residing for a significant portion of his life on the Aegean island of Chios, a crucial outpost for Venetian and Genoese trade, Bianco was a leading exponent of the portolan chart tradition. His work provided essential cartographic knowledge just as European powers were poised to embark on ambitious voyages of discovery, effectively bridging the practical demands of Mediterranean commerce with the emerging geographical curiosity of the Atlantic.

Bianco's most renowned achievement is his 1436 atlas, a collection of ten parchment leaves featuring detailed portolan charts of the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, and the Atlantic coastlines of Europe and North Africa. This atlas is notable for its inclusion of numerous islands, both real (such as the Azores and Canaries) and mythical (like Antillia and Brasil), reflecting the blend of known geography and speculative lore prevalent at the time. A later, single world map from 1448, now housed in the Biblioteca Marciana in Venice, further demonstrates his skill, uniquely depicting the coast of Scandinavia, Iceland, and Greenland with a surprising degree of accuracy, possibly drawn from Norse sagas or early fishing expeditions, and even indicating the legendary 'Dragon's Tail' off the coast of Asia.
